result:
Used books sometimes come with a second author. You find them in the margins: a pencil line beside a sentence, a question mark, an occasional "No!" pressed hard enough to dent the page. I love these people. They never expected an audience, so they're honest in a way the printed text can't be.

My favorite marginalia is the unscholarly kind: the grocery list on the flyleaf, the phone number with no name, the inscription reading "For David, who will understand chapter nine." Who was David? Did he understand? Chapter nine, when you get there, is about a man who leaves home and doesn't come back, and a paperback novel has become a small mystery with two plots.

There's a particular pleasure in disagreeing with a stranger's underlining. They marked the sentence about grief; you would have marked the one about the dog. You start building a picture of them (earnest, a little sad, bad at keeping pencils sharp) and it's certainly wrong, but it keeps you company.

Reading is described as a conversation between writer and reader. Marginalia makes it a three-way one, stretched across decades. The author spoke first, the stranger answered, and now you're listening in on both, free to add your own line.

I think that's why pristine books feel lonely. Nobody has argued with them yet. A marked-up copy has proof of life: someone was here and cared enough to push back.

So write in your books. Somebody in 2070 wants to know what you thought.
